title: Harvest-timed fertilizer offers in Busia: use without persistent adoption
summary: Research-assisted dose trials and randomised offers show that the configuration and timing of access matter; neither every recommended input package nor a universal present-bias account follows.

stages.feasibility: On-farm trials establish output and calculated returns for specific CAN doses, not fertilizer generically.
stages.deployment: SAFI sold vouchers at market fertilizer prices with free delivery at specified times.
stages.diffusion: Household any-plot use rose during treatment seasons.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Many eligible farmers did not buy; treatment effects did not persist into later seasons absent renewed offers.

counterevidence: Late-delivery estimate +9–10pp is imprecise, not zero; early–late contrast p=.08. More intensive official package had negative mean calculated return. Timing-choice result does not fully fit authors’ simple model.

episode.technology_configuration: Maize top-dressing CAN, with dose experiments distinguished from market-price fertilizer vouchers and delivery offers.
episode.task: Raise maize returns and arrange purchase before top-dressing time.
episode.population: Dose trials: farmers sampled via school-parent lists. SAFI: 1,230 farmers sampled from parents of fifth/sixth graders in 16 schools; outcome covers any household plot, not just respondent-controlled plots.
episode.interval: Six agronomic seasons starting July 2000; primary SAFI offers for 2004 long/short rains and follow-up in 2005.
contemporary_alternatives: No fertilizer or customary low input
Purchase fertilizer privately near application
Late free delivery
Late 50% subsidy
Early offer with chosen timing
episode.adoption_measure: Self-reported fertilizer use on any household plot by season. S01 Table 4 adjusted first-season effect +14.3pp against 24.0% comparison; adjusted second-season +18.1pp against about 26%. Denominators differ by season/controls (first-season full-controls N=716).
episode.observation_limits: Not a population diffusion curve; households without school-age pupils underrepresented; adoption data obtained for 924/1,230 sampled farmers (75.1%, S01 footnote10), with varying regression denominators and reporting limits; agronomic plots research-assisted.

actors.chooser: Sampled farmer accepts or refuses offer; household plot decisions may involve spouses.
actors.payer: Farmer pays fertilizer price; NGO funds delivery/experiment and the subsidy arm.
actors.operator_maintainer: Farmer/household applies inputs; field staff assist agronomic trials and deliver vouchers/fertilizer.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Other household cultivators and members bear resource allocation and farm-work consequences.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Explicit voluntary purchase; nonpurchase observed; fertilizer ownership allowed resale, although few reported it. Household members’ bargaining and independent refusal not measured.

labour.tasks: Input acquisition, transport, dose application, cultivation and harvest; delivery shifts a market trip to programme staff.
labour.entry_barriers: Cash/harvest resources, access to a market and plot, knowledge of dose; individual skill or land-access barriers not separately identified.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Private purchases and household plots; within-household control of gains not established.
labour.transition: Seasonal use observed; no permanent occupational transition followed.
labour.distribution: Dose-specific average returns and treatment averages; not effects on hired labour, landless people, wages or gendered task burdens.
labour.evidence_limit: Research-assisted plot profits and uptake cannot establish whole-farm livelihood gains or durable labour demand.

title: Learning which seaweed input to observe in Nusa Penida
summary: Farmers’ independently elicited knowledge differs by input dimension. A trial-plus-explanation package changes practices, but limited attention is not cleanly separated from computation, credibility or learning delay.

stages.feasibility: Existing seaweed farming; trials vary pod size and, in one arm, spacing.
stages.deployment: 117 farmers participate in compensated on-plot experiments followed by personalised summaries.
stages.diffusion: Only short-run within-sample input changes measured; no population spread estimate.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Trial participation before summaries produced little detectable change; spacing practices largely persisted.

counterevidence: Summary arrives later for all treated farmers, with no separate randomisation of timing/content. Measured pod-size effect about 7g is imprecise; explanation can change perceived returns as well as attention.

episode.technology_configuration: Existing line-grown seaweed with pod size and spacing as distinct adjustable inputs; 65 sorting trials and 52 weight trials.
episode.task: Choose productive planting inputs on a farmer’s own plot.
episode.population: 489 baseline respondents from a 2006 census of about 2,706 farmers in seven villages/24 hamlets; 117 randomly assigned trials; 232-person follow-up frame with 231 then 221 located.
episode.interval: Baseline June–December 2007; trials July 2007–March 2008; follow-ups April–May and July–August 2008, with summaries May–June.
contemporary_alternatives: Continue customary cutting/spacing
Learn by observing raw trial measurements
Use personalised summary and discussion
episode.adoption_measure: Enumerator-measured pod weights/distances and self-reported changed techniques. Table IV contains 684 person-wave observations, not 684 independent farmers.
episode.observation_limits: Short follow-up and selection of active existing growers; paper’s projected income gains are not sustained realised income measurements.

actors.chooser: Farm operator chooses subsequent inputs; assignment governs offer of researcher-managed trial.
actors.payer: Researchers provide trial inputs, guarantee a return floor and small time gift; farmer bears routine operating effort.
actors.operator_maintainer: Farmer and field team plant/weigh trial lines; subsequent cutting and cultivation remain farm tasks.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Household labour and buyers potentially affected; their outcomes not separately observed.
actors.ability_to_refuse: All approached trial farmers participated; voluntary context with compensation. Refusal by unpaid helpers or household members not measured.

labour.tasks: Cutting, attaching, sorting, measuring and tending seaweed; summary interpretation adds a knowledge task.
labour.entry_barriers: Existing farming plots/lines and practical knowledge; no new occupational entrants studied.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Farm-level decisions observed; ownership and sale of output not tested as bargaining mechanisms.
labour.transition: Two short follow-ups; no occupational migration or sustained skill-premium evidence.
labour.distribution: Input-dimension and trial-type heterogeneity; no robust gender/wealth distribution of livelihood gains established.
labour.evidence_limit: Labour cost of precise cutting and time spent interpreting evidence were not isolated experimentally.

title: Malawian agricultural communication: incentives, networks and gendered credibility
region: Malawi; eight-district extension experiment and three-district network experiment
summary: Public extension arrangements shape who communicates and receives attention. Targeting and incentives affect diffusion, but neither automatic peer imitation nor a uniform gender barrier to final uptake is established.

stages.deployment: Government extension officers train designated lead/peer farmers or two network-selected seeds.
stages.diffusion: Knowledge and observed/reported farming adoption followed over two or three seasons.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Non-incentivised dissemination often weak; benchmark network villages frequently show no non-seed adoption; most farmers remain non-adopters even with targeting.
stages.scaling: Expensive network mapping is a proof of concept, not a demonstrated cheap universal delivery system.

counterevidence: One versus five communicators confounds identity/coverage; S05/S06 share data. Network adoption-rate difference not significant in final year; reinforcement versus other multi-contact processes unresolved. Female-reserved roles yield poorer reception without a precise pooled downstream adoption/yield penalty.

episode.technology_configuration: Pit planting for maize moisture retention and crop-residue management; programmes and technologies kept separate where outcomes differ.
episode.task: Learn and disseminate cultivation methods through overstretched public extension.
episode.population: Programme A (S05/S06): 2009–11, eight districts; 120-village incentive/communicator analysis and overlapping 143-village gender-reservation analysis, rotating noncommunicator samples and separately interviewed spouses. Programme B (S04): 200 villages in Machinga, Mwanza, Nkhotakota, ~5,600 sampled households with network census covering >80% of households per village.
episode.interval: A: baseline 2009, follow-up 2010/2011. B: two or three annual rounds 2011–2013 depending on district.
contemporary_alternatives: Extension officer alone
One locally selected lead farmer
Five ordinary peer communicators with/without rewards
Two seeds selected by extension officer
Two seeds selected using network or geographic algorithms
Continue ridging/flat planting or alternative residue use
episode.adoption_measure: A: knowledge exams, contact/training reports and physical farm-practice checks; B: seasonal pit-planting adoption and village indicator for any non-seed adoption. Compare exact denominators and seasons, not pooled effect size.
episode.observation_limits: Rotating respondents/partial panels; network and incentive designs distinct. Most farmers never adopt within observation; weather and soil suitability differ.

actors.chooser: Ministry/researchers allocate communicator-selection rules; village meetings and officers select eligible people; each farmer decides subsequent practice.
actors.payer: Public extension and research programme support training and rewards; households provide cultivation resources.
actors.operator_maintainer: Extension officers, communicator farmers and household cultivators; communication is additional work.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Farm household members, unpaid workers and farmers not reached by extension.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Cultivation uptake not mandated; substantial non-adoption. Village role endorsement/selection documented; selected women’s within-household permission and cost of declining are not measured.

labour.tasks: Demonstration, explaining and answering questions; digging/reusing planting pits, weeding and residue management.
labour.entry_barriers: Lead criteria included literacy/status/resources; peer criteria broader. No gender gap in measured learning among selected communicators; female-led training receives less attendance.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Performance rewards acknowledge communication labour; who controls household gains and unpaid burdens is not established.
labour.transition: Communicator effort and farm tasks tracked over 2–3 seasons; not an occupational career panel.
labour.distribution: S06 directly measures sex-specific reception and subgroup knowledge/adoption; broad aggregate equivalence not proven. S05 reports labour-time changes but not wage or employment distribution.
labour.evidence_limit: No estimate of economy-wide extension job substitution, female earnings gains or landless-worker losses.

subepisodes.label: A: incentives and gender reservation
subepisodes.nonindependence: Overlapping cross-cutting experiment; do not count as two replications.

subepisodes.label: B: network selection
subepisodes.nonindependence: Separate design; same institutional/research context, community overlap not independently audited.

title: Hearing aids: service fit, identity and the difference between trying and keeping
region: United States; Indiana and San Francisco Bay Area
period: 2004–2008 observational cohort; one-year dyad study published 2010; clinical trial November 2012–August 2016 (published 2017)
summary: Task benefit, usage, identity and retention are distinct. Controlled delivery evidence and independently elicited interviews support a multi-part explanation, while price-cohort and selection limitations block a universal stigma or cost account.

stages.feasibility: Same digital hearing-aid hardware tested with effective amplification versus acoustically transparent placebo.
stages.deployment: Volunteers use audiology best-practice or consumer-selected preset fittings.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Some eligible volunteers decline trial purchase; some purchasers return devices; some interviewees discount stigma.
stages.displacement/reversal: Returns within one-month or six-plus-week trial windows observed; not long-term national abandonment.

counterevidence: Price assigned sequentially, not randomly; wealthy/educated clinic volunteers not representative. Daily use does not distinguish the randomised arms despite differences in benefits. Qualitative stigma lacks causal identification and is not universal.

episode.technology_configuration: S07: same digital mini-behind-ear aids with audiology best practices, consumer choice among presets or placebo programming; S08: earlier clinical hearing-aid purchase cohort; S09: help-seeking dyads discussing assorted aids.
episode.task: Everyday speech communication, not a generic normal-hearing restoration or cognition intervention.
episode.population: S07: 163 enrolled/154 completers, target ages 55–79 and mild-to-moderate hearing loss, no prior aid use, English native language and cognitive eligibility; 98% White,78% college degree,80% income >$45,000. S08: 139 never-users aged 60–89 in selected analytic comparison, 105 purchasers/34 nonpurchasers. S09: 91 dyads, hearing-impaired member >=60, 90% White, 84 followed to one year.
episode.interval: S08 original recruitment 2004–08; S09 one-year follow-up with field calendar dates unspecified; S07 trial recruitment/data collection 2 November 2012–31 August 2016, with six-week primary trial and optional four-week extension, published 2017.
contemporary_alternatives: No hearing aid or delayed purchase
Audiologist-selected/verified fitting with orientation
Consumer choice among preset aids
Communication adaptation by users/partners; not randomised as alternative
episode.adoption_measure: S07 speech/self-report benefit, satisfaction, datalogged daily hours, preliminary keep intention, later actual returns. S08 purchase decision and one-month returns. S09 narrated decisions and meanings; no population uptake denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Three distinct study populations; no pooled rate. Placebo trial and interview evidence address different questions. Severe loss, cognitive/dexterity barriers and Deaf identity not represented by these samples.

actors.chooser: Adults elect trial participation and retention; service model randomised after consent. Dyad partners influence discussions but do not necessarily choose devices.
actors.payer: Trial participants pay device charge; research support covers trial infrastructure. In S07 typical/reduced prices occur sequentially.
actors.operator_maintainer: Wearer inserts/cleans devices and changes batteries; audiologists fit and troubleshoot; partners adapt communication.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Communication partners bear repetition, relationship and communication costs.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Nonparticipation and returns documented; consent and refund options available. Clinical recommendation does not establish a duty to adopt; constrained alternatives for severe impairment outside scope.

labour.tasks: Audiometry, fitting, orientation, maintenance and user self-management; unpaid communication adaptation by partners.
labour.entry_barriers: Clinical credentials for providers; for users hearing configuration, cognition/language eligibility and payment. Severe dexterity barriers mostly excluded/unmeasured.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Users buy and can return aids; professional versus self-service tasks reorganised, not provider earnings measured.
labour.transition: Weeks to one year for use/decisions; no professional displacement or job-transition panel.
labour.distribution: Predominantly White selected older volunteers; lower-income, working-age and non-English users insufficiently covered.
labour.evidence_limit: No claim about labour-market benefits, optimal lifetime use, all assistive technologies or all deaf/hard-of-hearing people.

title: Bicycles and girls’ schooling: distinct Bihar and Zambia institutional packages
period: Bihar 2006–2008 with later exam checks; Zambia 2017–2021
summary: Two explicitly separate school-access episodes show that finance, infrastructure, maintenance and gendered circumstances jointly shape mobility. Neither identifies a universal psychological effect of a bicycle or of paying for it.

stages.deployment: Bihar cash earmarked for bicycle purchase; Zambia distributed bikes with mechanics, monitoring and school-use custody conditions.
stages.diffusion: Bihar programme exposure affects grade-age enrolment; Zambia randomised school offer affects access, travel and attendance. These are not comparable bike-ownership diffusion curves.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Those outside school/distance eligibility are largely unobserved; distant girls retain constraints; several agency and educational outcomes have null/imprecise effects.
stages.scaling: Bihar is statewide programme evaluation; Zambia is a 100-school trial. No extrapolated national saturation claim.

counterevidence: Bihar schooling/safety reforms and roads are rival/complementary processes; norm change not separately measured. Road proxy is imperfect/nonrandom. In the May2025 Zambia manuscript, fee/free-arm differences and pooled general mobility/aspirations are imprecise while selected reported agency outcomes improve. The final abstract says educational aspirations improved; final tables/definitions and pooled-versus-arm-specific interpretation were not inspected, so this difference remains unresolved.

episode.technology_configuration: Bihar: Rs2,000 earmarked grant after grade-9 enrolment, school receipt certification. Zambia: durable bicycle plus trained mechanic, supervisory committee and four-year resale prohibition, with randomised $5 maintenance-fee versus free variants.
episode.task: Access school and reduce commuting burdens for adolescent girls; ownership and broader mobility are separate outcomes.
episode.population: Bihar: DLHS-3 household members age14–17, treated age14–15 versus16–17, girls versus boys, Bihar versus Jharkhand; full-control main Table2 N=30,112. Zambia: 100 public basic schools, initially enrolled grade5–7 girls walking >3km away; urban and some very remote schools excluded. 25 payment, 20 free, 55 control schools. Survey frame2,471; Table1 commute N=1,879 and Table4 attendance N=1,952.
episode.interval: Bihar grant launched June2006; DLHS late2007/early2008. Zambia baseline July–August2017, distribution September–November2017, follow-up October–December2018, administrative follow-up2019–21.
contemporary_alternatives: Walking to existing school
Do not enrol or discontinue schooling
Other transport where available, not a uniform available substitute
School construction/relocation not randomised in these studies
Zambia otherwise identical bike package with/without nominal fee
episode.adoption_measure: Bihar age-appropriate enrolment/completion proxy from policy exposure (+5.2pp in main adjusted estimate), not measured riding. Zambia self-reported access, minutes one-way and days absent/late last week, plus agency indices; later administrative retention/attendance conditional samples separate.
episode.observation_limits: No pooled effect/denominator. Bihar triple-difference assumptions; Zambia differential attrition and self-report, later administrative data not preregistered. Final Zambia full text not acquired: detailed evidence from May2025 manuscript; its imprecise pooled aspirations differ from the final abstract’s positive assertion, unresolved until final tables/definitions are inspected. Disability/cycling-ability representation and route accessibility not established; no such exclusion rule identified in inspected sampling passages.

actors.chooser: Governments/NGO define eligibility and conditions; households choose Bihar purchase/type; Zambia girls/guardians accept allocated bikes and girls operate them subject to family and school rules.
actors.payer: Bihar state funds grant; households may cover extras/maintenance. Zambia programme funds bicycles/support; treatment families pay nominal maintenance fee only in payment arm.
actors.operator_maintainer: Girls ride; families share some use; Bihar local repair arrangements unmeasured; Zambia school-linked trained mechanics support repair.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Household members, excluded/out-of-school girls, siblings and school staff; sharing and monitoring can redistribute resources/control.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Zambia refusal reported but almost universal take-up among eligible recipients; primary-school use and resale restrictions limit subsequent choice. Bihar household discretion/receipt conditions documented; adolescent bargaining or independent refusal not fully measured.

labour.tasks: Travel time shifts; bicycle repair/supervision tasks; household asset-sharing. Zambia Table2 lower odds of girls’ income-generating time but no clear changes in most other reported time categories.
labour.entry_barriers: Documented Zambia eligibility is school enrolment in grades5–7 and walking distance; school sampling excludes urban and some very remote schools. Disability, cycling capacity and route accessibility are unmeasured applicability limits here, not established eligibility rules; household permission may constrain use.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Bihar grant earmarked to eligible girls; Zambia conditional custodianship and household sharing. Selected self-reported bargaining improves, not unrestricted asset control.
labour.transition: School outcomes followed up to four years; adult employment, wages and occupation transitions not established.
labour.distribution: Gender targeted; distance heterogeneity and imperfect road-connected comparisons. Out-of-school/noneligible girls outside Zambia target; disability/cycling-ability representation and corresponding outcomes not established.
labour.evidence_limit: School participation or agency scores cannot be converted into future earnings, occupational access or universal emancipation.

subepisodes.label: Bihar quasi-experiment
subepisodes.population: Age14–17 Bihar/Jharkhand cohorts; no pooled Zambia denominator.

subepisodes.label: Zambia school-randomised comparison
subepisodes.population: Initially enrolled grade5–7 girls >3km from100 schools.
